summary.text: Measuring earthquakes means giving each quake a magnitude, a number for its overall strength or size, as opposed to intensity, which rates how hard the ground shakes at one spot.
Magnitude is usually worked out from seismic waves on a seismogram, by measuring things like a wave's timing, amplitude, frequency or duration.
Every magnitude scale keeps Richter's logarithmic design, where one unit means ten times the wave amplitude and roughly 32 times the energy.

items.prompt: During one quake, a town built on thick soft fill shakes far harder than a town on firm rock the same distance away. What is different between the two towns?

options.label: The size of the fault rupture

items.explain: Magnitude describes the quake as a whole; intensity is the shaking at a given place, and soft soil can amplify the waves.

items.prompt: A magnitude 7 quake is compared with a magnitude 6 quake. Roughly how much more seismic energy does the bigger one release?
items.explain: Each unit is ten times the wave amplitude, and since energy grows with amplitude to the power 1.5, that is about 32 times the energy.

items.prompt: In the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake, San Francisco's Marina district was among the worst-hit areas despite lying nearly 100 km from the epicenter. What best explains this?

options.label: Soft ground there amplified the waves
The epicenter moved toward the city
Magnitude grew as the waves travelled
A separate quake struck the district

items.explain: Local shaking depends heavily on soil, and thick soft layers such as fill can amplify seismic waves far from the source.

items.prompt: Why do seismologists use several magnitude scales instead of just one?

options.label: Each country keeps its own scale by law
Each scale rates a different kind of damage
Quakes, available data and purposes differ

items.explain: Scales differ in which part of the waves they measure, because earthquakes, the information on hand and the uses of the number all vary.

items.prompt: A seismologist estimates a very large quake's size using only one part of its seismic wave-train. What is the typical risk?
items.explain: Measuring only part of the wave-train leaves the picture incomplete and can systematically underestimate magnitude, a problem called saturation.

items.prompt: A short-period scale using P waves was set up with a worldwide seismograph network in the 1960s. Besides catching smaller events, what did it help tell apart from tectonic earthquakes?
items.explain: The mb scale's short period improves detection of small events and better separates tectonic earthquakes from underground nuclear explosions.
